claims.text: Atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility govern the reliable formation and catalytic performance of noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
Atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility influence HEA phase stability.
Atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility influence the distribution of catalytic active sites.
Changing combinations of Au, Pt, Pd, Rh, Ir, Cu, Ni, and Co can systematically vary atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility.
Atomic size mismatch affects lattice strain.
Atomic size mismatch affects phase stability.
Electronic-structure compatibility influences the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The electronic density of states at the Fermi level affects catalytic activity and selectivity.
HEA nanomaterials with moderate atomic size mismatch and high electronic-structure compatibility will have higher phase stability than HEAs with extreme mismatch or poor compatibility.

HEA nanomaterials with moderate atomic size mismatch and high electronic-structure compatibility will have a more uniform distribution of active sites than HEAs with extreme mismatch or poor compatibility.
HEA nanomaterials with moderate atomic size mismatch and high electronic-structure compatibility will deliver superior catalytic performance to HEAs with extreme mismatch or poor compatibility.
HEA nanomaterials with minimal atomic size mismatch and high electronic compatibility are expected to have optimal phase stability and catalytic performance.
The proposed relationship applies when synthesis permits sufficient atomic diffusion and mixing.
The proposed relationship applies to catalytic reactions sensitive to electronic structure and active-site distribution.
Optimal quantitative thresholds for atomic size mismatch and electronic compatibility may depend on the catalytic reaction.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome identifies moderate atomic size mismatch as favorable relative to extreme mismatch, whereas the baseline identifies minimal mismatch as optimal. The hypothesis does not explain whether minimal or moderate mismatch is the expected optimum.
